title: Children's Room Design: Key Principles | DUMSKAYA DESIGN
description: How to design a child's room: safety, zoning, furniture that grows with the child, light and colour. Key rules from DUMSKAYA DESIGN.

parts.html: A children’s room has to be safe and change as the child grows: what works for a three-year-old gets in the way at ten. Below are the rules we follow when designing children’s rooms.
Age: The needs of an infant, a preschooler, and a school-age child differ greatly. Keep in mind that a toddler needs more room to play, while a schoolchild needs a place to study.
Interests: Ask your child what they are into. A child who draws needs a big desk and space for paper, a musician needs a corner for the instrument, and a sporty kid needs a wall bar.
Zoning: Divide the room into zones for sleeping, playing, and studying.
Function: The sleeping area should be calm and dark, with heavy curtains and away from the toys. The play area goes closer to the light, with a soft floor covering and nothing fragile.
Ergonomics: Choose furniture to suit your child’s height: a desk and chair appropriate for their age, and shelves within easy reach.
Color palette: Keep the main finishes in calm, neutral colors and add bright accents with decor and textiles. Bright colors suit the play area; calm ones suit the sleeping area.
Lighting:
Natural light: Let as much daylight into the room as possible.
General lighting: Create even lighting with ceiling fixtures.
Zone lighting: Add reading lamps next to the bed, as well as a desk lamp on the desk.

Materials: Use washable water-based paint on the walls, wood or cork on the floor, and boards with low formaldehyde emissions (class E1) for furniture. Choose washable curtains and rugs: dust builds up quickly in a child’s room.
Furniture: Avoid sharp corners and check that large pieces are stable. If your child is young, be sure to anchor cabinets and shelves to the walls.
Electrical: Fit all outlets with safety covers and hide the cables.
Bed: For toddlers, choose beds with side rails to prevent falls. For school-age children, beds with storage drawers are a good fit.

Storage: Toys are easiest to keep in open bins and baskets on the lower shelves so the child can take them out and put them away on their own. For clothes and books, a wardrobe and modular shelving that can be rearranged or extended as the child grows.
Multifunctional furniture: If space is tight, choose furniture that serves several purposes — for example, a bed with a work area or a folding table.
Textiles: Cushions, rugs, and curtains are the simplest way to add color, and they are easy to change when your child’s tastes change.

Personal touches: Let your child pick some things themselves: the color of one wall, the bedding, a poster of their favorite characters. That way the room becomes theirs, and these things are cheap to replace later.
Modularity: Keep in mind that your child’s needs will change. Use modular systems that can easily be adapted to new purposes.
Room to grow: Leave some free space so you can add new elements over time, such as a study area or extra storage.
Details: A shelf where books face cover-out, a wall with chalkboard or magnetic paint for drawing on and pinning up pictures: these are things a child uses every day.

Ideas: Pictures from magazines and design websites are a good starting point, but check each one against your own room: whether there is enough space, whether it suits your child’s height, and whether it is easy to clean.
A good children’s room fits the child’s height and age, has space for sleeping, playing, and studying, and can be reworked without a renovation as the child grows.
